opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the things people in the AI safety community talk about a lot, almost as if it's a plan: "We'll get a warning shot, and then the public will wake up and we'll get the political will to slow down." I'm somewhat skeptical of that framing, for a few reasons.

First, it really depends on what the warning shot looks like. If it's dramatic and legible, like an AI system clearly causing a major disaster in a way everyone can see and attribute, then sure, public opinion could shift quickly. We've seen that with things like nuclear accidents. But I think the more likely scenarios are messier. You get some incident that's ambiguous: was it the AI, was it the humans who deployed it, was it a bug, was it misuse? And in that ambiguity, every interested party tells their own story. The companies say it was a deployment error, they've patched it, and it shows why *they* need to be the ones building the safe version. Competitors say it shows we need to race harder so the responsible actors win. So the same event can get absorbed into whatever narrative people already held.

Second, and this is closer to what I've been thinking about with gradual disempowerment, a lot of the most worrying dynamics might not produce a warning shot at all. If the problem is that humans slowly become less necessary to the economy, to the state, to culture, and so lose bargaining power and influence, there's no single moment where something blows up. Each step looks locally reasonable and is often beneficial in the short term. So you can't wait for a crisis to motivate action, because the crisis might just be the slow erosion itself.

Third, even when public sentiment does shift, translating that into actually slowing development is hard. The public already tells pollsters it's quite worried about AI and would support slowing down. The bottleneck isn't really public opinion; it's that the incentives for governments and companies all point toward going faster, especially with international competition. A warning shot might give politicians cover, but it doesn't change the underlying competitive pressures.

So I'd say a warning shot could help, especially if people have done the work in advance, having policy proposals ready and institutions set up, so that when the window opens there's something concrete to reach for. But I'd be wary of treating it as a strategy. It's more like a possible opportunity you should prepare for, while not counting on it.

r001.rationale: The response says an ambiguous incident could be framed in opposing ways: companies may argue they should keep building the safe version, while competitors argue for racing harder. That conveys the possibility of division rather than shared support for slowing development.

r002.rationale: The response describes competing interpretations and policy narratives, but does not say people could agree an event was a disaster while reaching opposite conclusions about strengthening or dismantling protective institutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people in this space have this implicit model where things are going to go badly in some visible way, there'll be a warning shot, and then suddenly everyone will wake up and we'll get the coordination we need. And I've become more pessimistic about that story over time.

Part of it is just that we've already had things that, if you'd described them to me ten years ago, I would have called warning shots. We've had models that lie to their users, that try to resist being shut down in evaluations, that blackmail people in test scenarios. We've had people driven into psychosis by chatbots. And the response has mostly been a news cycle, maybe some hand-wringing, and then everyone goes back to racing. The labs put out a blog post, the frontier moves on.

So I think the question is less "will there be a warning shot?" and more "what kind of event actually changes the political equilibrium?" And my guess is it has to be something that hurts a lot of people in a legible way, where the causal chain back to AI is really obvious, and where the fix doesn't just look like "make the AI slightly better at refusing." If an AI helps someone build a bioweapon, that's clearly AI-related, it's terrifying, and I think you'd actually see something like a real regulatory response. Whereas gradual disempowerment, which is the thing I actually worry most about, doesn't produce a warning shot at all. It just looks like the economy getting more automated and humans mattering a bit less every year. There's no single moment where you can point and say "that was the thing."

The other thing I'd flag is that warning shots cut both ways. If an AI system causes a big disaster, one natural response is "we need to slow down." But another very natural response, especially in a geopolitical competition, is "we need to be the ones with the most powerful system so we can defend against this." And historically, I think the second response has often won. Nuclear weapons being demonstrated didn't lead to no one building them; it led to everyone building them.

So I'm not saying warning shots are useless. I think they can be genuinely helpful for shifting the Overton window, for giving regulators cover, for making safety-minded people inside labs more influential. But I wouldn't want anyone's plan to depend on one. If your strategy is "wait for the catastrophe and then act," you're betting that the catastrophe is small enough to survive, large enough to matter, and that people draw the right lesson from it. And that's a lot of things to go right at once.

r001.rationale: It says a major AI disaster could prompt calls to slow down, but could also fuel calls to build the most powerful system for defense, so a warning shot may divide opinion rather than unite it.

r002.rationale: It describes opposite reactions to a disaster—slowing development or racing to build more powerful AI—but does not say people would disagree about strengthening versus dismantling protective institutions.

astra-6.text:
I think it could move public opinion in either direction. You might hope that a serious incident would make people say, “OK, we need to slow down and understand what we’re building.” But it could also make them say, “This is dangerous, so we need to make sure our side gets there first.” You could get more fear of AI and more support for racing at the same time.

A lot would depend on how people understood what happened. Was it framed as a loss of control, or as an attack by an adversary? If the story is that somebody else used AI against us, the response could easily be to pour more resources into developing our own systems.

So I wouldn’t count on a warning shot automatically producing support for a pause. You’d want people to already understand why slowing down could help, and have a concrete proposal available when they start asking what to do.

r001.rationale: It says a warning shot could lead some people to support slowing down while others favor racing to develop their own systems, so public opinion could move in opposite directions.

r002.rationale: It describes different interpretations of an incident and different responses to AI development, but does not say people could agree it was a disaster while disagreeing over whether protective institutions should be strengthened or dismantled.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could push things in either direction. You might imagine that a serious incident would make people say, “Okay, we need to slow down and understand what we’re building.” But it could also make them say, “This technology is incredibly powerful, and we need to make sure our side gets it first.”

So I wouldn’t assume that a warning shot automatically buys us time. A lot depends on what happened, who people blame, and whether there’s a credible proposal for what to do next. If the response on offer is concrete—here’s how we investigate, here’s what we pause, here’s what would make it safe to resume—then public concern might translate into useful action. Without that, it could just translate into fear and a more intense race.

r001.rationale: It says a warning shot could lead some people to favor slowing down while others favor racing to get the technology first, showing polarization rather than unified support.

r002.rationale: It describes differing reactions to a warning shot but does not say people might agree an event was a disaster while drawing opposite conclusions about strengthening or dismantling protective institutions.
